Chapter Details: The architecture, governance, functionality and uptake of government digital identity systems and credentials. 30 variables in 5 sections. Contains latest available data. Data collection by Perplexity from a variety of sources.
Definition: Whether individuals can view their data held in the ID database and see how it has been accessed
Comments: No right or mechanism for individuals to view/access their data stored in Sudan's ID system has been documented. The Data Protection Africa fact sheet confirms 'Right of data subject to access a copy of their personal data: No law.' The Civil Registry operates without documented citizen data access portals. SudaPass plans are not specific about individual data access rights.
revision_notes: Original score of 1 (No mechanism) rested on the 2022 Data Protection Africa factsheet and pre-launch uncertainty about SudaPass. SudaPass, Sudan's national digital identity platform operated by the National Authority for Digital Certification, launched in Khartoum on 21 May 2026. Its published privacy policy (sudapass.gov.sd/privacy) explicitly states individuals have the right to 'Access your personal data, Correct inaccurate data, Delete your data, Withdraw consent', and the app itself functions as a self-service digital identity wallet. This is a documented self-service access mechanism that did not exist at the time of the original assessment. Score raised to 2 (Yes).
revised_comments: Individuals can access their personal data held in Sudan's digital identity system. SudaPass, the national digital identity platform launched in May 2026 and operated by the National Authority for Digital Certification, provides a self-service mobile app functioning as a digital identity wallet, and its published privacy policy grants users the right to access, correct, delete and withdraw consent for their personal data. No equivalent access mechanism is documented for the underlying civil registry database itself.

Definition: Whether the system enables Know Your Customer (KYC) packet collection for service provision, particularly financial services
Comments: KYC using the national ID is enabled in Sudan. The UNCDF report confirms 'the police manage the national ID platform, accessible to MNOs for KYC purposes and used by the credit bureau during the credit-scoring process.' Financial institutions use the national ID number for customer identification as required by the AML/CTF Act 2014 and CBOS regulations. However, the UNCDF also notes that full digital e-KYC platforms are yet to be developed, and KYC currently relies largely on physical document checks.
revision_notes: Confirmed. The 2023 UNCDF assessment already documented use of the national ID for MNO and credit-bureau KYC. This is now reinforced by SudaPass (launched May 2026), which offers 'National Number Verification' and passport/biometric-based identity verification explicitly designed for third-party authorisation of banks and other service providers, moving Sudan's KYC process toward a genuine e-KYC capability.
revised_comments: Know Your Customer processes in Sudan are enabled through the national identity system. Financial institutions and mobile network operators use the national identity number for customer identification, as required under the AML/CTF Act 2014 and Central Bank of Sudan regulations. The SudaPass digital identity platform, launched in May 2026, extends this with app-based National Number and passport verification and biometric authentication, allowing banks and other service providers to conduct third-party identity checks electronically.

Definition: Whether the ID authority and system are subject to general oversight of the courts and judicial review
Value Name: Yes, but not specific to ID
Comments: Sudan's constitution (Section 55) protects the right to privacy including correspondence, which provides a general constitutional basis for judicial oversight of identity systems. The general court system can in principle be used to challenge identity-related decisions. However, no ID-specific judicial oversight mechanisms have been documented. Assessed as 'Yes but not ID-specific' based on general constitutional protections without dedicated mechanisms.
revision_notes: Confirmed. No ID-specific judicial review mechanism is documented in any source reviewed, including recent (2025-2026) surveys of Sudan's digital governance institutions, which describe new cybersecurity, data and AI, and digital transformation authorities but no ID-specific tribunal or appeals mechanism. General constitutional privacy protection and the ordinary court system remain the only avenue, consistent with the original assessment.
revised_comments: Sudan's identity system is subject to general judicial oversight rather than ID-specific mechanisms. The constitutional protection of privacy (under the 2019 Constitutional Charter) provides a basis for challenging identity-related decisions through the ordinary court system, but no dedicated ID tribunal, appeals body or ID-specific judicial review mechanism has been established.

Definition: Whether the civil registration and digital ID systems are integrated
Comments: The 2011 civil registry reform integrated civil registration with the national ID system — registration requires proof of birth/citizenship, and the national identity number is needed to obtain civil documents (birth certificate, marriage certificate). The UN Sudan presentation (2018) confirms the Civil Registry database tracks births, deaths, marriages, divorces for continuous updating. However, the World Bank SFSP project (2020) identifies NCR links to administrative databases as still being strengthened, and fragmentation remains an issue. Partial integration assessed.
revision_notes: Confirmed. The 2011 civil registry reform remains the backbone linking birth/citizenship records to the national identity number. SudaPass, launched May 2026, is implemented 'in partnership with the Ministry of Interior, represented by the Civil Registry' (Sudan Events, 21 May 2026), confirming continued but partial integration rather than a fully unified system; registries are still described elsewhere (WEF, Jan 2026) as fragmented, with ministries using different identifiers.
revised_comments: Sudan's civil registration and identity systems are partially integrated. Registration in the civil registry, introduced in 2011, is the basis for issuance of the national identity number and subsequent civil, identity and travel documents. SudaPass, the national digital identity platform launched in May 2026, is delivered in partnership with the Civil Registry under the Ministry of Interior. Registries nonetheless remain fragmented across government agencies, with ministries using different identifiers and humanitarian actors maintaining parallel databases.

Definition: Whether procedural rules for collection, storage, and sharing of ID-related personal data are publicly available and established
Comments: Sudan has no formal data sharing rules for the ID system. The Data Protection Africa fact sheet confirms there are 'no laws restricting cross-border transfer' and no requirements for data sharing notifications, data processing registers, or related frameworks. The UNCDF payment infrastructure report notes the police manage the national ID platform accessible to MNOs for KYC without mention of structured data sharing rules.
revision_notes: Original score of 1 (Not available) reflected the absence of published rules as at 2022. SudaPass, launched May 2026, publishes a privacy policy (sudapass.gov.sd/privacy) setting out categories of data collected, purposes of use, storage/security measures, and data-subject rights, and describes a consent-based mechanism for authorising third-party access. This constitutes publicly available procedural rules, though only for the new digital layer; no equivalent published rules were found for the broader civil registry/police-held identity data. Score raised to 2 (Partially available).
revised_comments: Procedural rules for the collection, storage and sharing of digital identity data are partially available in Sudan. SudaPass, the national digital identity platform launched in May 2026, publishes a privacy policy describing the categories of personal and biometric data collected, its use, security measures and data-subject rights, and provides a consent-based mechanism through which citizens authorise third parties such as banks and government agencies to access their data. No equivalent published data-sharing framework is documented for the underlying civil registry system.

Definition: Whether national data protection legislation exists and covers personal data linked to the ID system
Comments: Sudan has no data protection legislation. The Data Protection Africa fact sheet confirms: 'Sudan currently has no data protection legislation, although various sectoral laws are of relevance, such as the Electronic Transactions Act 2007, Cybercrime Act 2018, Cybercrime Prevention (Amendment) Act 2020, and Law No. 14 on Information Technology Crime.' A Draft Data Protection Bill was proposed in 2018 but remained in draft form as of research date.
revision_notes: Confirmed. Multiple 2026 legal trackers confirm Sudan still has no comprehensive data protection statute; the 2018 Draft Data Protection Bill remains unenacted. Sudan signed the AU Malabo Convention on Cyber Security and Personal Data Protection in March 2023 but has not ratified it (confirmed as of February 2026).
revised_comments: Sudan has no comprehensive data protection legislation. Personal data protection is addressed only indirectly through constitutional privacy provisions and sectoral laws such as the Electronic Transactions Act 2007 and the Cybercrime Act 2018/2020. A Draft Data Protection Bill proposed in 2018 has not been enacted. Sudan signed the African Union Malabo Convention on Cyber Security and Personal Data Protection in March 2023 but has not yet ratified it.

Definition: Whether a Data Protection Authority or similar body regulates ID data collection and sharing by the ID system
Comments: Sudan has no Data Protection Authority. The Data Protection Africa fact sheet confirms: 'no data protection authority yet appointed'. While the National Information Center (NIC) oversees some data-related matters and three new digital authorities were established in November 2025 (Digital Transformation Authority, Sudan Data and AI Authority, Cybersecurity Authority), none functions as a formal DPA with individual rights enforcement powers.
revision_notes: Confirmed. No dedicated Data Protection Authority exists. In November 2025 Sudan established three new bodies (Digital Transformation Authority, Sudanese Data and AI Authority, Sudanese Cybersecurity Authority) with roles in national data governance and cybersecurity, but none is a data-protection authority with individual-rights enforcement powers; a 2026 review (levellers.ai) confirms no dedicated national data-protection authority is publicly documented.
revised_comments: Sudan has no Data Protection Authority regulating ID data collection and sharing. Three new digital governance bodies were established in November 2025 — the Digital Transformation Authority, the Sudanese Data and AI Authority, and the Sudanese Cybersecurity Authority — with mandates covering data governance and cybersecurity, but none functions as a dedicated authority enforcing individual data-protection rights over the identity system.

Definition: Whether the digital ID credential serves as legal proof of an individual's identity as codified in law
Comments: The national ID card and national identity number issued under the Civil Registration Act 2011 serve as legal proof of identity in Sudan. The ID card is required for formal employment (Article 27.3), opening bank accounts, obtaining passports, and other legal purposes. The US State Department and IRB Canada confirm the national ID card/number is the primary legal identity document.
revision_notes: Confirmed. The national identity card/number issued under the Civil Registration Act 2011 remains the primary legal proof of identity. The launch of SudaPass in May 2026, which verifies identity against the National Number and e-passport, reinforces rather than replaces this legal basis; no source indicates a change in the credential's legal status.
revised_comments: The national identity card and identity number issued under the Civil Registration Act 2011 serve as legal proof of identity in Sudan and are required for formal employment, banking and other legal purposes. The credential retains this status under the new SudaPass digital identity platform, which authenticates users against their existing national identity number or passport.

Definition: Whether formal legislation (act, law, regulation) governs digital identity including identification acts, digital ID laws, or equivalent legislation
Comments: Sudan has a legal framework for its identity system. The Civil Registration Act 2011 mandates civil registration, assignment of the national identity number, and obliges citizens over 16 to obtain an ID card. The Electronic Transactions Act 2007 and Cybercrime Act 2018 provide additional legal underpinning for digital identity activities.
revision_notes: Confirmed. The Civil Registration Act 2011 remains the core legislation. Digital-ID-specific regulation is now also evidenced by the Regulation for Organising Certification for Electronic Certification Service Providers 2018, which underpins the National Authority for Digital Certification and the SudaPass platform launched in 2026.
revised_comments: Sudan's identity system operates under formal legislation. The Civil Registration Act 2011 mandates civil registration and issuance of the national identity number, with citizens over 16 obliged to obtain an ID card. Digital identity activities are further underpinned by the Electronic Transactions Act 2007 and the 2018 Regulation for Organising Certification for Electronic Certification Service Providers, which governs the National Authority for Digital Certification responsible for the SudaPass platform.

Definition: Whether the system and the production of credentials can be managed, maintained and developed by in-country technical staff (as opposed to foreign vendors)
Comments: The civil registry is managed domestically by the General Directorate of Civil Registration (Ministry of Interior). However, the payment infrastructure involves Gemalto's Mobile Payment Platform (GMPP) operated by Electronic Banking Services (EBS), indicating some foreign vendor involvement in ID-adjacent systems. The new SudaPass system has not yet disclosed its technology vendor. Assessed as partial in-country maintenance given mixed domestic/foreign components.
revision_notes: Confirmed at partial in-country capacity. The Sudanese Cybersecurity Authority states (29 May 2026) that SudaPass is 'developed and operated by Sudanese professionals and experts', but this is a single self-reported government statement without independent verification, and the National Authority for Digital Certification separately discloses a partnership with the foreign firm Sectigo for browser-trusted root certificate services. Score not upgraded to 'All in-country' on this evidence alone; retained at partial in-country capacity.
revised_comments: Sudan's identity system is maintained through a mix of domestic and foreign technical capacity. The civil registry is managed domestically by the General Directorate of Civil Registration. The Sudanese Cybersecurity Authority states that the new SudaPass digital identity platform is developed and operated by Sudanese professionals, while the National Authority for Digital Certification maintains a partnership with an international certificate authority (Sectigo) for globally trusted digital certificates, indicating continued reliance on foreign infrastructure for some functions.

Definition: Whether the Ministry of Finance has oversight of the financing and development of the digital ID system
Comments: The Ministry of Finance and Economy oversees the Sudan Family Support Program (SFSP), which uses the national civil registry identity platform for digital delivery of cash transfers. The World Bank Sudan Family Support Project (2020) describes the Ministry of Finance's role in the program linked to national ID. However, no comprehensive evidence of full Ministry of Finance oversight of the ID system itself was found.
revision_notes: Confirmed. No fresher evidence located on Ministry of Finance oversight of the identity system specifically; SudaPass is administered by the Ministry of Digital Transformation and Communications and the Sudanese Cybersecurity Authority, not the Ministry of Finance, while the Ministry of Finance and Economic Planning continues to oversee the Sudan Family Support Program that relies on the national civil registry platform.
revised_comments: The Ministry of Finance and Economic Planning has partial oversight of Sudan's identity ecosystem. It oversees the Sudan Family Support Program, which uses the national civil registry identity platform for beneficiary validation and cash-transfer delivery. The identity system itself, including the SudaPass digital identity platform, is administered by the Ministry of Digital Transformation and Communications and the Ministry of Interior's Civil Registry, with no comprehensive evidence of full Ministry of Finance budgetary oversight of the ID system.

Definition: Whether the system collects biometric data and which modalities are collected (fingerprints, facial image, iris scans)
Comments: Sudan's civil registry records fingerprints from all applicants aged 12+ and facial photos at enrollment. The Civil Registration Act 2011 mandates in-person registration with fingerprint recording. The new SudaPass platform is planned to use facial biometrics (face recognition via passport/selfie). Iris scans are not documented as part of the standard system. Classified as 'Facial/Iris' tier (value=3) based on fingerprints + facial photo at minimum.
revision_notes: Confirmed and strengthened. SudaPass, launched May 2026, uses facial photograph matching against the e-passport NFC chip plus a live selfie, and offers Face ID/fingerprint passwordless authentication, corroborating the facial/fingerprint biometric tier already recorded for the civil registry. No iris capture is documented.
revised_comments: Sudan's identity system collects fingerprint and facial biometric data. The civil registry records fingerprints from applicants aged 12 and above and a facial photograph at enrolment. The SudaPass digital identity platform, launched in May 2026, verifies users by matching a live selfie against the facial photograph stored on the e-passport chip and supports Face ID/fingerprint-based passwordless authentication. Iris capture is not documented.

Definition: Whether identity records are stored in electronic/digital format versus paper-based records
Comments: Sudan introduced a new electronic and centralised civil registry in 2011, replacing the old hand-written and decentralised registers. The database is digital and centrally managed by the General Directorate of Civil Registration under the Ministry of Interior. Each citizen receives a unique 11-digit national identity number linked to biometric data stored digitally.
revision_notes: Confirmed. The centralised electronic civil registry introduced in 2011 remains digital, and is now overlaid by the SudaPass digital identity platform (launched May 2026), reinforcing the fully electronic nature of the underlying identity records.
revised_comments: Identity records in Sudan are stored electronically. The centralised civil registry, introduced in 2011 to replace paper-based registers, holds digital records tied to a unique national identity number and biometric data. The SudaPass digital identity platform, launched in 2026, provides an additional electronic layer for identity verification and credential storage.

Definition: Whether the digital ID system is designed to be interoperable across government agencies and with other systems through APIs or data exchange protocols
Comments: Sudan's civil registry database is used by ID and passport offices for verification via the national identity number, and the police manage the national ID platform accessible to MNOs and the credit bureau for KYC. However, multiple sources describe registries as fragmented with ministries using different identifiers and humanitarian agencies running parallel databases. The WEF (2026) notes 'registries remain fragmented' and the UNCDF (2023) notes 'CBOS could enhance interoperability between separate systems'. Full system interoperability has not been achieved.
revision_notes: Original score of 1 (No) reflected the fragmented, pre-launch state of Sudan's registries. SudaPass, launched May 2026, is explicitly described by its operator (Sudanese Cybersecurity Authority) as providing 'system integration and connection with government and service systems', and its published app features include 'Third-Party Authorization: Safely authorize government services, banks, and businesses to verify your identity' — a documented authorisation-based interoperability mechanism. Score raised to 2 (Yes). Note that WEF (Jan 2026) still describes underlying registries as fragmented, so interoperability is limited to what SudaPass itself connects to at launch.
revised_comments: Sudan's digital identity system is designed to be interoperable across government agencies and with other service providers. SudaPass, launched in May 2026, provides third-party authorisation functionality that allows government services, banks and businesses to verify a user's identity electronically with the user's consent, and its operator describes the platform as enabling system integration and connection with government and service systems. Underlying civil, humanitarian and ministerial registries remain only partially aligned.

Definition: Whether credential is accepted or mandatory for opening bank accounts and accessing financial services
Comments: The national ID number is required (mandatory) to open a bank account in Sudan. The Landinfo (2023) report and IRB Canada confirm the national identity card/number is required for banking. The UNCDF (2023) report confirms KYC for financial services relies on the national ID number, and the IRB Canada source explicitly states 'identity cards are required...except for some circumstances such as posting bail and opening a bank account.'
revision_notes: Confirmed. No evidence found that this requirement has changed; the national identity number remains mandatory for opening bank accounts, and SudaPass now offers an additional digital channel for this same identity verification.
revised_comments: The national identity number is mandatory for opening a bank account and accessing financial services in Sudan. Financial institutions rely on the national identity number for customer identification and KYC, a requirement now also supported through the SudaPass digital identity platform for electronic verification.

Definition: Whether credentials are issued free of charge
Comments: The ID card in Sudan involves fees. The Landinfo (2023) report notes that the ID card is 'expensive to obtain' with many Sudanese choosing not to get one and instead using other official documents containing their national identity number. The UNCDF Sudan payment infrastructure report confirms the NID card is mandatory but the application process involves costs. The new SudaPass digital platform is announced as free (Ministry of Digital Transformation confirmed it 'shall be free'), but this refers to the new system not yet deployed.
revision_notes: Ambiguous. The original score of 1 (No) rested on the physical national ID card being 'expensive to obtain' (Landinfo 2023). SudaPass, Sudan's new digital identity credential, launched in May 2026 and is confirmed free of charge in multiple sources ('The service is free for all users', Sudan Horizon, Dec 2025; Biometric Update, Feb 2026). However, SudaPass registration is activated using an existing passport or National Number, both of which derive from the underlying fee-based national ID/passport system, so registering 'from scratch' may still involve a cost. Given the genuine interpretive question of which credential the variable is scored against, and no independent evidence resolving whether SudaPass activation is possible without a pre-existing paid credential, this is flagged for human review rather than asserted either way.
revised_comments: The cost of obtaining an identity credential in Sudan differs by system. The physical national ID card, issued under the Civil Registration Act 2011, involves fees that Landinfo describes as a barrier for some citizens. SudaPass, the digital identity platform launched in May 2026, is explicitly advertised as free to use, though activation depends on an individual already holding a passport or national identity number.

Definition: Age in years at which an individual becomes eligible to register for digital ID
Comments: Under the Civil Registry Act 2011, ID cards are issued to Sudanese citizens over 16. The Landinfo (2023) report and IRB Canada (2013) confirm mandatory ID card acquisition at age 16 (Article 27.1). Children under 16 can be registered in the civil registry (birth registration), but the ID card itself requires age 16+. Fingerprints recorded from age 12. Scored as '>17' = 1, but clarification: the threshold is 16, which falls in the '>17' equivalent zone since enrollment for the physical ID credential starts at 16.
revision_notes: Corrected. Both cited sources (Landinfo 2023; IRB Canada 2013) agree that the identity card is mandatory from age 16 under the Civil Registration Act 2011 (Article 27.1). On the variable's scale (1 = >17; 2 = 10-17; 3 = 6-10; 4 = 1-5; 5 = <1), an eligibility age of 16 falls within the '10-17' band, i.e. code 2, not code 1 (>17) as originally recorded. The original comments themselves noted the discrepancy but the Value Code was not adjusted to match. Code corrected to 2 to match the cited evidence.
revised_comments: Individuals become eligible for a mandatory identity card at age 16 under Sudan's Civil Registration Act 2011 (Article 27.1). Birth registration in the civil registry can occur earlier, but issuance of the identity card itself is tied to the age-16 threshold. Fingerprints are recorded from age 12 as part of the registration process.

revision_notes: Confirmed. The Civil Registration Act 2011 (Article 27.1) continues to mandate ID card acquisition for all citizens aged 16 and above; no legislative change found.
revised_comments: Registration for the national identity card is mandatory for all Sudanese citizens aged 16 and above under the Civil Registration Act 2011 (Article 27.1). Enforcement varies across the country, particularly in conflict-affected areas, but the legal requirement applies universally to citizens above the eligibility age.

Comments: The IRB Canada source (citing the Sudanese Embassy official) states that 'national identity cards are not required to access public health care, and patients can provide their nationality cards if requested.' This suggests the national ID/nationality card is accepted but not strictly mandatory for healthcare. Scored as 'Accepted not mandatory' based on this evidence.
revision_notes: Confirmed. No fresher evidence located specifically on ID requirements for healthcare access; the sole cited source (a 2013 Sudanese Embassy statement to IRB Canada) remains the only documented evidence and indicates the ID is accepted, not mandatory, for public healthcare.
revised_comments: The national identity card is accepted but not mandatory for accessing public healthcare services in Sudan; patients may provide the card if requested but it is not a strict prerequisite for treatment. This remains the only documented position on the question, based on a statement from Sudanese consular officials, and may not reflect any changes to hospital registration practice since 2013.

Definition: Whether non-nationals including refugees, asylum seekers, and permanent residents are eligible to register
Comments: The Civil Registry Act 2011 (Article 34.2) provides for an 'alien's identity card' for foreigners residing in Sudan. UNHCR Khartoum representative confirmed registered South Sudanese in Khartoum were issued identification cards by the aliens department and police. However, the national identity number and full national ID are for Sudanese citizens only. Some non-nationals (registered aliens, refugees with UNHCR registration) can get a form of ID.
revision_notes: Confirmed. No fresher evidence found; the Civil Registration Act 2011 (Article 34.2) continues to provide for an 'alien's identity card', and registered refugees/asylum seekers can obtain some form of identification, but the full national ID/National Number remains restricted to citizens.
revised_comments: Some categories of non-nationals are eligible for identification in Sudan. The Civil Registration Act 2011 provides for an alien's identity card for foreign residents, and registered refugees have historically been issued identification by the aliens department and police. The full national identity number and national ID remain restricted to Sudanese citizens.

Chapter Details: The architecture, governance, functionality and uptake of government digital identity systems and credentials. 30 variables in 5 sections. Contains latest available data. Data collection by Perplexity from a variety of sources.
Definition: Percentage of eligible population that has been issued or registered with digital ID credentials
Comments: According to the IFC report, the national civil registry includes 33 million unique names representing 75-80% coverage (among the highest in Africa). The Landinfo (2023) report cites 82% in 2016 and 35.5/40 million (88.75%) in 2021 per government officials. Conflict and displacement since April 2023 (civil war) may have reduced effective coverage. IFC notes expansion to 90% was planned under SFSP. The 75-80% figure from IFC most credibly represents pre-conflict coverage — scored as 50-69% given post-conflict disruption, or conservatively at 3 (50-69%). Given 2021 official data of ~88%, and accounting for the 2023+ crisis, a value of 3 (50-69%) to 4 (70-89%) is defensible; scored 3 (50-69%) to be conservative given ongoing conflict impacts.
revision_notes: Confirmed but genuinely uncertain. No authoritative post-conflict figure for national ID/civil registry coverage was located; the World Bank ID4D database's latest Global Findex-based adult ID ownership update (2024 release) was checked but did not return a Sudan-specific figure in the available preview. The most recent adult-coverage estimate remains approximately 89% (35.5m/40m, 2021, pre-conflict), while UNICEF-sourced birth registration (a different, child-focused metric) was only 24.0% in 2022, illustrating how uneven coverage is by age group and region. The conflict since April 2023 has displaced over 10 million people and disrupted civil registry operations, and SudaPass (the new digital layer) has enrolled only a small fraction of the population so far (100K+ app installs against a population of roughly 51 million by June 2026). The original estimate of 50-69% is retained as a reasonable band rather than the higher pre-war figure, but this remains a judgement call in the absence of a verified current registration rate, so it is flagged for human review.
revised_comments: Coverage of Sudan's national identity system is substantial but uneven and likely reduced by ongoing conflict. Pre-conflict government figures put registration at around 89% of the eligible population (35.5 million of 40 million, 2021), with coverage historically lower in Darfur and other peripheral, conflict-affected areas. The war since April 2023 has displaced over 10 million people and disrupted civil registry operations in several states, while the new SudaPass digital identity platform, launched in 2026, has so far reached only a small fraction of the population. No authoritative post-conflict national coverage figure is currently available.

Definition: Whether credential is accepted or mandatory for SIM card activation and mobile service registration
Comments: SIM card registration is mandatory in Sudan. A 2021 study cited by GNI confirmed SIM card registration is mandatory in Sudan. The PikaSim eSIM provider confirms 'Sudan requires national ID or passport registration for all SIM cards.' The uqudo report references Telecommunications and Post Regulatory Authority (TPRA) requirements for SIM registration. MNOs access the national ID platform for KYC per the UNCDF report.
revision_notes: Confirmed. No fresher evidence found; mandatory SIM registration against the national ID remains in force, reinforced by SudaPass extending KYC/ID verification capability.
revised_comments: SIM card registration is mandatory in Sudan and requires the national identity card or number. Mobile network operators verify subscriber identity against the national ID platform under Telecommunications and Post Regulatory Authority requirements, with the national identity number serving as the basis for KYC checks.

Definition: Whether credential is accepted or mandatory for registering for social assistance programs and accessing social services
Comments: The Sudan Family Support Program (SFSP), a major World Bank-supported cash transfer program targeting 80% of the population (6.5 million families), uses the National Civil Registry identity platform for beneficiary validation and digital delivery of payments. The World Bank Project Appraisal Document (2020) confirms NCR validation is mandatory for SFSP registration. Additionally, formal employment requires a national ID number (Civil Registry Act 2011, Article 27.3).
revision_notes: Confirmed. The Sudan Family Support Program continues to validate beneficiaries against the National Civil Registry platform; no evidence of a change to this requirement, and SudaPass may extend this validation channel further given its integration with the Civil Registry.
revised_comments: National civil registry identification is mandatory for enrolment in Sudan's major social protection programme. The World Bank-supported Sudan Family Support Program validates beneficiaries against the National Civil Registry platform before delivering cash transfers, and formal employment separately requires a national identity number under the Civil Registration Act 2011.
